en: Saṃyutta Nikāya 14.1 (SN 14.1, PTS SN ii 140) 1. The Chapter on Diversity The Discourse on the Diversity of Elements At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, there is a diversity of elements. What is that diversity of elements? It is the eye-element, the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element; the ear-element, the sound-element, the ear-consciousness-element; the nose-element, the odor-element, the nose-consciousness-element; the tongue-element, the flavor-element, the tongue-consciousness-element; the body-element, the tactile-object-element, the body-consciousness-element; the mind-element, the mental-phenomena-element, the mind-consciousness-element. This is called the diversity of elements.”
Staying at Sāvatthī, [the Blessed One said]: “Monks, I will teach you the diversity of elements.
Listen to it and attend closely; I shall speak.”
“Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“And what, bhikkhus, is the diversity of elements?
The eye element, the form element, the eye-consciousness element; the ear element, the sound element, the ear-consciousness element;
the nose element, the odor element, the nose-consciousness element; the tongue element, the flavor element, the tongue-consciousness element;
the body element, the tangible-object element, the body-consciousness element; the mind element, the mental-phenomena element, the mind-consciousness element.
“This, monks, is called the diversity of elements. Thus was it said.

*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 14.2. (SN 14.2, PTS SN ii 140)
1. The Chapter on Diversity:
Discourse on the Diversity of Contact.
At Sāvatthī, [the Blessed One] was dwelling.
“Monks, dependent on the diversity of elements arises the diversity of contact.
And what, monks, is the diversity of elements?
The eye element, the ear element, the nose element, the tongue element, the body element, and the mind element.”
This, monks, is called the diversity of elements.
And how, monks, does the diversity of contact arise in dependence on the diversity of elements?
In dependence on the eye-element, monks, arises eye-contact.
Dependent on the ear-element … dependent on the nose-element … dependent on the tongue-element …
“Dependent on the body-element ...
dependent on the mind-element, mind-contact arises.
It is in this way, monks, that diversity of contact arises in dependence on diversity of elements.”
The Second.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 14.3 (SN 14.3, PTS SN ii 141) 1.
The Chapter on Diversity (Nānattavagga)
The Discourse on the Diversity of Contact. At Sāvatthī, the Blessed One was staying there.
“Monks, it is in dependence upon the diversity of elements that the diversity of contact arises; it is not in dependence upon the diversity of contact that the diversity of elements arises.”
And what, bhikkhus, is the diversity of elements?
The eye-element … [and so on] … the mind-element.

This, monks, is called the diversity of elements (*dhātunānatta*). And how, monks, does the diversity of contact (*phassanānatta*) arise dependent on the diversity of elements, but the diversity of elements not arise dependent on the diversity of contact? Dependent on the eye-element (*cakkhudhātu*), monks, arises eye-contact; eye-contact does not arise dependent on eye-contact... [and so forth] ...up to: dependent on the mind-element arises mind-contact; mind-contact does not arise dependent on mind-contact. This, monks, is called the diversity of elements. And how, monks, does the diversity of feeling (*vedanānānatta*) arise dependent on the diversity of contact, but the diversity of contact not arise dependent on the diversity of feeling? Dependent on eye-contact, monks, arises feeling born of eye-contact; feeling born of eye-contact does not arise dependent on feeling born of eye-contact... [and so forth] ...up to: dependent on mind-contact arises feeling born of mind-contact; feeling born of mind-contact does not arise dependent on feeling born of mind-contact. This, monks, is called the diversity of feeling. And how, monks, does the diversity of perception (*saññānānatta*) arise dependent on the diversity of feeling, but the diversity of feeling not arise dependent on the diversity of perception? Dependent on feeling born of eye-contact, monks, arises perception associated with feeling born of eye-contact; perception associated with feeling born of eye-contact does not arise dependent on perception associated with feeling born of eye-contact... [and so forth] ...up to: dependent on feeling born of mind-contact arises perception associated with feeling born of mind-contact; perception associated with feeling born of mind-contact does not arise dependent on perception associated with feeling born of mind-contact. This, monks, is called the diversity of perception. And how, monks, does the diversity of volitional formations (*saṅkhāranānatta*) arise dependent on the diversity of perception, but the diversity of perception not arise dependent on the diversity of volitional formations? Dependent on perception associated with feeling born of eye-contact, monks, arises volitional formation associated with perception associated with feeling born of eye-contact; volitional formation associated with perception associated with feeling born of eye-contact does not arise dependent on volitional formation associated with perception associated with feeling born of eye-contact... [and so forth] ...up to: dependent on perception associated with feeling born of mind-contact arises volitional formation associated with perception associated with feeling born of mind-contact; volitional formation associated with perception associated with feeling born of mind-contact does not arise dependent on volitional formation associated with perception associated with feeling born of mind-contact. This, monks, is called the diversity of volitional formations. And how, monks, does craving (*taṇhā*) arise dependent on the diversity of volitional formations, but the diversity of volitional formations not arise dependent on craving? Dependent on volitional formations associated with perception associated with feeling born of eye-contact, monks, arises craving for volitional formations associated with perception associated with feeling born of eye-contact; craving for volitional formations associated with perception associated with feeling born of eye-contact does not arise dependent on volitional formations associated with perception associated with feeling born of eye-contact... [and so forth] ...up to: dependent on volitional formations associated with perception associated with feeling born of mind-contact arises craving for volitional formations associated with perception associated with feeling born of mind-contact; craving for volitional formations associated with perception associated with feeling born of mind-contact does not arise dependent on volitional formations associated with perception associated with feeling born of mind-contact. This, monks, is called the diversity of craving. And how, monks, does clinging (*upādāna*) arise dependent on craving, but craving not arise dependent on clinging? Dependent on craving for volitional formations associated with perception associated with feeling born of eye-contact, monks, arises clinging to volitional formations associated with perception associated with feeling born of eye-contact; clinging to volitional formations associated with perception associated with feeling born of eye-contact does not arise dependent on craving for volitional formations associated with perception associated with feeling born of eye-contact... [and so forth] ...up to: dependent on craving for volitional formations associated with perception associated with feeling born of mind-contact arises clinging to volitional formations associated with perception associated with feeling born of mind-contact; clinging to volitional formations associated with perception associated with feeling born of mind-contact does not arise dependent on craving for volitional formations associated with perception associated with feeling born of mind-contact. This, monks, is called the diversity of clinging. And how, monks, does becoming (*bhava*) arise dependent on clinging, but clinging not arise dependent on becoming? Dependent on clinging to volitional formations associated with perception associated with feeling born of eye-contact, monks, arises becoming in volitional formations associated with perception associated with feeling born of eye-contact; becoming in volitional formations associated with perception associated with feeling born of eye-contact does not arise dependent on clinging to volitional formations associated with perception associated with feeling born of eye-contact... [and so forth] ...up to: dependent on clinging to volitional formations associated with perception associated with feeling born of mind-contact arises becoming in volitional formations associated with perception associated with feeling born of mind-contact; becoming in volitional formations associated with perception associated with feeling born of mind-contact does not arise dependent on clinging to volitional formations associated with perception associated with feeling born of mind-contact. This, monks, is called the diversity of becoming. And how, monks, does birth (*jāti*) arise dependent on becoming, but becoming not arise dependent on birth? Dependent on becoming in volitional formations associated with perception associated with feeling born of eye-contact, monks, arises birth in volitional formations associated with perception associated with feeling born of eye-contact; birth in volitional formations associated with perception associated with feeling born of eye-contact does not arise dependent on becoming in volitional formations associated with perception associated with feeling born of eye-contact... [and so forth] ...up to: dependent on becoming in volitional formations associated with perception associated with feeling born of mind-contact arises birth in volitional formations associated with perception associated with feeling born of mind-contact; birth in volitional formations associated with perception associated with feeling born of mind-contact does not arise dependent on becoming in volitional formations associated with perception associated with feeling born of mind-contact. This, monks, is called the diversity of birth. And how, monks, does aging-and-death (*jarāmaraṇa*) arise dependent on birth, but birth not arise dependent on aging-and-death? Dependent on birth in volitional formations associated with perception associated with feeling born of eye-contact, monks, arises aging-and-death in volitional formations associated with perception associated with feeling born of eye-contact; aging-and-death in volitional formations associated with perception associated with feeling born of eye-contact does not arise dependent on birth in volitional formations associated with perception associated with feeling born of eye-contact... [and so forth] ...up to: dependent on birth in volitional formations associated with perception associated with feeling born of mind-contact arises aging-and-death in volitional formations associated with perception associated with feeling born of mind-contact; aging-and-death in volitional formations associated with perception associated with feeling born of mind-contact does not arise dependent on birth in volitional formations associated with perception associated with feeling born of mind-contact. This, monks, is called the diversity of aging-and-death. This, monks, is the diversity of elements. This, monks, is the diversity of contact. This, monks, is the diversity of feeling. Saṁyutta Nikāya 14.4 (SN 14.4, PTS SN ii 141) 1. Nānattavagga Vedanānānattasutta: The Discourse on the Diversity of Feelings "Bhikkhus, there are these three kinds of feeling. What three? Pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. These, bhikkhus, are the three kinds of feeling. When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: "But, Bhante, what is the cause, what is the condition, for the diversity of these three feelings? "Bhikkhu, contact is the cause, contact is the condition, for the diversity of these three feelings. "But, Bhante, what is the cause, what is the condition, for the diversity of contacts? "Bhikkhu, the diversity of elements is the cause, the diversity of elements is the condition, for the diversity of contacts. "But, Bhante, what is the cause, what is the condition, for the diversity of elements? "Bhikkhu, it is, by way of convention, that I speak of the diversity of elements; for, bhikkhu, apart from conventional designation, I do not see any phenomenon that is a 'diversity of elements'. When this was said, that bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: "Magnificent, Bhante! Magnificent, Bhante! It is as if, Bhante, one were to set upright what had been overturned, or to reveal what was hidden, or to show the way to one who was lost, or to bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms. Just so, Bhante, the Blessed One has made the Dhamma clear in many ways. I go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Sangha of bhikkhus. May I receive the going forth under the Blessed One, may I receive the higher ordination! Then that bhikkhu received the going forth under the Blessed One; he received the higher ordination. And soon, not long after his higher ordination, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, that bhikkhu realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, that unsurpassed consummation of the spiritual life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness, and having entered upon it, he dwelt therein. He directly knew: "Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being. And that venerable one became one of the arahants.
At Sāvatthī, the Blessed One was staying.
“Monks, dependent on the diversity of elements arises the diversity of contact; dependent on the diversity of contact arises the diversity of feeling.
And what, monks, is the diversity of elements?”
The eye element …pe… the mind element—
this, monks, is called the diversity of elements. And how, monks,
does the diversity of contact arise in dependence on the diversity of elements, and how does the diversity of feeling arise in dependence on the diversity of contact?
“Dependent on the eye-element, monks, arises eye-contact; dependent on eye-contact, arises feeling born of eye-contact.
…pe… Dependent on the mind-element, arises mind-contact; dependent on mind-contact, arises feeling born of mind-contact.
It is in this way, monks, that diversity of elements gives rise to diversity of contact, and diversity of contact gives rise to diversity of feeling.”

Saṁyutta Nikāya 14.5 (SN 14.5, PTS SN ii 142) 1.
The Chapter on Diversity (Nānattavagga)
The Second Discourse on the Diversity of Feelings. At Sāvatthī.
“Bhikkhus, in dependence on the diversity of elements there arises the diversity of contact; in dependence on the diversity of contact, [there arises the diversity of feeling].”
The diversity of feelings arises; it is not that the diversity of feelings arises dependent on the diversity of contact;
nor does the diversity of contact arise dependent on the diversity of feelings.
And what, bhikkhus, is the diversity of elements?
The eye element …pe… the mind element—this, monks, is called the diversity of elements.
And how, monks, does the diversity of contact arise in dependence on the diversity of elements? The diversity of contact—

“Dependent on what does the diversity of feelings arise, and not dependent on the diversity of feelings does the diversity of contacts arise, and not dependent on the diversity of contacts does the diversity of elements arise?
Monks, dependent on the eye-element arises eye-contact; dependent on eye-contact...”
Feeling born of eye-contact arises; eye-contact does not arise dependent on feeling born of eye-contact.
Eye-element does not arise dependent on eye-contact...
[and so on] ...mind-element arises dependent on mind-contact; mind-contact arises dependent on feeling born of mind-contact.
Feeling; feeling does not arise dependent on mind-contact, nor does mind-contact arise dependent on mind-contact, nor does the mind-element arise dependent on mind-contact.
Thus, monks, dependent on the diversity of elements arises the diversity of contact, and from the diversity of contact...
“Dependent upon diversity of contact, diversity of feeling arises; it is not that diversity of feeling arises dependent upon diversity of contact.
Dependent upon diversity of elements, diversity of contact arises; it is not that diversity of contact arises dependent upon diversity of elements.
The fifth.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 14.6 (SN 14.6, PTS SN ii 143) 1. The Chapter on Diversity The Discourse on the Diversity of External Elements "Bhikkhus, there are these six external elements.
What six? The earth element, the water element, the fire element, the air element, the space element, and the consciousness element. These, bhikkhus, are the six external elements."

At Sāvatthī, the Blessed One was staying. “Monks, I will teach you the diversity of elements. Listen to that... [as before]... [The Buddha said: “Monks, there are these six elements. Which six? The earth element, the water element, the fire element, the air element, the space element, and the consciousness element. These, monks, are the six elements. “Monks, there are these eighteen mental explorations. Which eighteen? When one explores a visible form with the eye, there is an exploration accompanied by pleasure, an exploration accompanied by pain, and an exploration accompanied by equanimity. When one explores a sound with the ear... a smell with the nose... a taste with the tongue... a tactile object with the body... a mental phenomenon with the mind, there is an exploration accompanied by pleasure, an exploration accompanied by pain, and an exploration accompanied by equanimity. These, monks, are the eighteen mental explorations. “Monks, there are these nine progressive dwellings. Which nine? Here, monks, a bhikkhu dwells having attained the first jhāna. From that he emerges and dwells having attained the second jhāna. From that he emerges and dwells having attained the third jhāna. From that he emerges and dwells having attained the fourth jhāna. From that he emerges and dwells having attained the base of infinite space. From that he emerges and dwells having attained the base of infinite consciousness. From that he emerges and dwells having attained the base of nothingness. From that he emerges and dwells having attained the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. From that he emerges and dwells having attained the cessation of perception and feeling.

These, monks, are the nine progressive dwellings. “Monks, there are these four modes of practice. Which four? The mode of practice leading to the pleasant now and ripening in the future; the mode of practice leading to pain now and ripening in the future; the mode of practice leading to pain now and ripening in the present; and the mode of practice leading to the pleasant now and ripening in the present. These, monks, are the four modes of practice. “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. Which four? Here, monks, some person is intent on his own welfare but not on the welfare of others. Some person is intent on the welfare of others but not on his own welfare. Some person is intent neither on his own welfare nor on the welfare of others. And some person is intent both on his own welfare and on the welfare of others. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. Which four? Here, monks, some person is blameworthy in both this world and the next. Some person is blameworthy in this world but praiseworthy in the next. Some person is praiseworthy in this world but blameworthy in the next. And some person is praiseworthy both in this world and in the next. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. Which four? Here, monks, some person is a destroyer of life, a taker of what is not given, unchaste in sexual conduct, a speaker of falsehood, and one who partakes of intoxicants that cause heedlessness. Some person is a destroyer of life, a taker of what is not given, unchaste in sexual conduct, a speaker of falsehood, and one who does not partake of intoxicants that cause heedlessness. Some person is not a destroyer of life, a taker of what is not given, unchaste in sexual conduct, a speaker of falsehood, and one who partakes of intoxicants that cause heedlessness. And some person is not a destroyer of life, a taker of what is not given, unchaste in sexual conduct, a speaker of falsehood, and one who does not partake of intoxicants that cause heedlessness. Saṁyutta Nikāya 14.7 (SN 14.7, PTS SN ii 143) 1.
The Chapter on Diversity (Nānattavagga)
The Discourse on the Diversity of Perceptions. At Sāvatthī, the Blessed One was staying there.
“Monks, it is in dependence upon the diversity of elements that the diversity of perceptions arises; in dependence upon the diversity of perceptions,” [he said].
Diversity of intention arises; dependent on diversity of intention, diversity of desire arises;
dependent on diversity of desire, diversity of passion arises; dependent on diversity of passion, diversity of seeking arises.
And what, bhikkhus, is the diversity of elements?
The element of form …pe… the element of mental phenomena—this, monks, is called the diversity of elements.
And how, monks, does the diversity of perceptions arise in dependence on the diversity of elements? The diversity of perceptions …pe… [as above].
“Dependent upon what does diversity of intention arise? Dependent upon diversity of intention does diversity of desire arise.
Dependent upon diversity of desire does diversity of fever arise. Dependent upon diversity of fever does diversity of seeking arise?
Monks, dependent upon the form element does perception of form arise; dependent upon perception of form does [diversity of intention arise].”
There is intention regarding forms; dependent on intention regarding forms, desire for forms arises; dependent on desire for forms, fever for forms arises;
dependent on fever for forms, the search for forms arises...
[and so on] ...dependent on the element of mental phenomena, perception of mental phenomena arises; dependent on perception of mental phenomena, intention regarding mental phenomena arises.
Dependent on a thought of phenomena, desire for phenomena arises; dependent on desire for phenomena, fever for phenomena arises;
dependent on fever for phenomena, the search for phenomena arises.
Thus, monks, dependent on the diversity of elements, the diversity of perceptions arises; [dependent on] the diversity of perceptions...
“Dependent upon diversity of intention, diversity of desire arises;
dependent upon diversity of desire, diversity of passion arises; dependent upon diversity of passion, diversity of seeking arises.”
Seventh.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 14.8 (SN 14.8, PTS SN ii 144) 1.
The Chapter on Diversity (Nānattavagga)
The Discourse on the Diversity of Searches. At Sāvatthī.
“Bhikkhus, dependent on the diversity of elements arises the diversity of perceptions; dependent on the diversity of perceptions, [arises the diversity of intentions].”
The diversity of intentions arises; dependent on the diversity of intentions, the diversity of desires arises;
dependent on the diversity of desires, the diversity of fevers arises; dependent on the diversity of fevers, the diversity of quests arises.
It is not that the diversity of fevers arises dependent on the diversity of quests, nor that the diversity of fevers arises dependent on the diversity of fevers.
“Diversity of desire arises; diversity of intention does not arise dependent on diversity of desire. Diversity of perception arises;
diversity of intention does not arise dependent on diversity of perception. Diversity of elements arises; diversity of perception does not arise dependent on diversity of elements.
And what, bhikkhus, is the diversity of elements?”
The element of form …pe… the element of mental phenomena—this, monks, is called the diversity of elements.

And how, monks, does the diversity of perceptions arise in dependence on the diversity of elements? In dependence on the diversity of perceptions, [the diversity of intentions arises] …pe… [and so on] … the diversity of quests.
Is it not the case that diversity of fever does not arise in dependence on diversity of search; that diversity of desire does not arise in dependence on diversity of fever;
that diversity of intention does not arise in dependence on diversity of desire;
that diversity of perception does not arise in dependence on diversity of intention; and that diversity of elements does not arise in dependence on diversity of perception?
“Bhikkhus, dependent on the form element, perception of forms arises … dependent on the mental-object element, perception of mental objects arises;
dependent on the perception of mental objects, [craving for mental objects arises] … dependent on the search for mental objects, fever for mental objects does not arise;
dependent on fever for mental objects, [suffering does not arise].”
The desire for the Dhamma arises; dependent on the desire for the Dhamma, the intention for the Dhamma does not arise;
dependent on the intention for the Dhamma, the perception of the Dhamma does not arise; dependent on the perception of the Dhamma, the element of the Dhamma does not arise.

Thus, monks, dependent on the diversity of elements, the diversity of perceptions arises; dependent on the diversity of perceptions, [the diversity of intentions arises] …pe… [and so on] … up to the diversity of quests.
“Diversity of fever does not arise in dependence on diversity of pursuit; diversity of desire does not arise in dependence on diversity of fever;
diversity of intention does not arise in dependence on diversity of desire;
diversity of perception does not arise in dependence on diversity of intention; and diversity of elements does not arise in dependence on diversity of perception.”
Eighth.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 14.9 (SN 14.9, PTS SN ii 146) 1.
The Chapter on Diversity (Nānattavagga)
The Discourse on the Diversity of External Contacts. At Sāvatthī.
“Monks, it is in dependence upon the diversity of elements that the diversity of perceptions arises; in dependence upon the diversity of perceptions...”
The diversity of intentions arises; dependent on the diversity of intentions, the diversity of contacts arises;
dependent on the diversity of contacts, the diversity of feelings arises; dependent on the diversity of feelings, the diversity of desires arises;

wrong speech … wrong action … wrong livelihood …

The Third Chapter on the Paths of Action.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 14.30 (SN 14.30, PTS SN ii 169).
4. The Fourth Chapter.
The Discourse on the Four Elements.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery… “Bhikkhus,
there are these four elements.
“What four? The earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element—
these, monks, are the four elements.”
First.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 14.31 (SN 14.31, PTS SN ii 169) 4.
Fourth Chapter (Catutthavagga)
The Pubbeva Sambodha Sutta.
[The Blessed One] was dwelling at Sāvatthī.
“Monks, before my full enlightenment, while I was still an unenlightened Bodhisatta, this occurred to me:”
‘What, then, is the gratification, what is the danger, and what is the escape in the case of the earth element?
What is the gratification, what is the danger, and what is the escape in the case of the water element?
What is the gratification, what is the danger, and what is the escape in the case of the fire element?’
‘What is the gratification, what is the danger, and what is the escape in the air element?
Then, monks, this occurred to me:
‘Whatever pleasure and joy arise in dependence on the earth element—this is the gratification in the earth element.’”
That the earth element is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—this is the danger in the earth element.
The removal of desire and lust for the earth element, the abandoning of desire and lust for the earth element—this is the escape from the earth element.
That which depends on the water element … [and so forth] …
Whatever pleasure and joy arise in dependence on the fire element...
or whatever pleasure and joy arise in dependence on the air element—this is the gratification in the air element;
that the air element is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—this is the danger in the air element.
‘The removal of desire and lust for the air element, the abandoning of desire and lust for the air element— this is the escape from the air element. Monks,
as long as I did not directly know these four elements as they really are— in their gratification as gratification, in their danger as danger,
and in their escape as escape— I did not, monks, [claim to have awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment].”
In this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans,
I claimed to have fully awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
And from the time, monks, that I had thus seen the gratification in these four elements as gratification and the danger in them as danger...
When I had directly known, as they really are, the escape from what is dangerous and the danger in the escape, then, monks,
I claimed to have awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans.
"And knowledge and vision arose in me:
‘My liberation is unshakable; this is my last birth; now there is no further becoming. This is the second [sutta].

Saṁyutta Nikāya 14.32 (SN 14.32, PTS SN ii 171) 4. Catutthavagga Acariṁsutta “Bhikkhus, I shall teach you the noble method of practice. Listen to that and attend closely; I will speak. “Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, here a noble disciple has heard thus: ‘The Noble Ones practice in such a way, they train themselves in such a way, they dwell with their minds well-restrained by such things. He practices in such a way, trains himself in such a way, and dwells with his mind well-restrained by such things. This, bhikkhus, is called the noble method of practice. And what, bhikkhus, is the noble method of practice? Here, bhikkhus, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Enlightened One, the Blessed One. He possesses confirmed confidence in the Dhamma thus: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. He possesses confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha thus: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. He possesses the virtues dear to the Noble Ones, unbroken, untorn, unblemished, unmottled, freeing, praised by the wise, ungrasped, leading to concentration. This, bhikkhus, is called the noble method of practice.”

At Sāvatthī, the Blessed One was staying. “Monks, I set out in search of the gratification in the earth element. Whatever gratification there is in the earth element, I attained it; whatever gratification there is in the earth element, that has been well-seen by me through wisdom.

Monks, I set out in search of the danger in the earth element. Whatever danger there is in the earth element, I attained it; whatever danger there is in the earth element, that has been well-seen by me through wisdom.”

“Bhikkhus, I set out in search of the escape from the earth element; I attained that which is the escape from the earth element, and I have clearly seen with wisdom that which is the escape from the earth element as far as it extends.
Bhikkhus, I set out in search of the escape from the water element... from the fire element...”

“Bhikkhus, I set out seeking the gratification in the air element; I discovered whatever gratification there was in the air element, and to whatever extent there is gratification in the air element, that has been clearly seen by me with wisdom.

Bhikkhus, I set out seeking the danger in the air element; I discovered whatever danger there was in the air element, and to whatever extent there is danger in the air element, that has been clearly seen by me with wisdom.”

“Bhikkhus, I set out in search of the escape from the air element; I attained that escape from the air element, and as far as there is an escape from the air element, that was well seen by me through wisdom.

Bhikkhus, as long as I did not directly know, as they really are, the gratification in these four elements as gratification, the danger as danger, and the escape as escape, for so long, bhikkhus, I did not [claim full enlightenment].”
In this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans,
I claimed to have awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
And from the time, monks, that I had understood the gratification as gratification and the danger as danger regarding these four elements...
When I had directly known, as they really are, the escape from what is dangerous and the danger in the escape, then, monks,
I claimed to have awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans.
And knowledge and vision arose in me:
‘Unshakable is my liberation; this is my last birth; now there is no more renewed existence. Thus it was for the third time.

Saṁyutta Nikāya 14.33 (SN 14.33, PTS SN ii 172) 4. Catutthavagga Nocedaṁ Sutta “Bhikkhus, if this were not, there would not be for the arising of this world; if this did not exist, this world would not be manifest. What is that? If name-and-form were not, there would not be for the arising of this world; if name-and-form did not exist, this world would not be manifest. Therefore, bhikkhus, it is by means of name-and-form as condition that consciousness comes to be; by means of consciousness as condition, name-and-form; by means of name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases; by means of the six sense bases as condition, contact; by means of contact as condition, feeling; by means of feeling as condition, craving; by means of craving as condition, clinging; by means of clinging as condition, existence; by means of existence as condition, birth; by means of birth as condition, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come to be. Such is the origin of this whole mass of suffering. “If, bhikkhus, there were no fuel at all in the world, would there be the manifestation of fire? “No, venerable sir. “Therefore, bhikkhus, it is by means of fuel as condition that fire comes to be; by means of fire as condition, smoke and sparks. Thus, bhikkhus, it is by means of name-and-form as condition that consciousness comes to be; by means of consciousness as condition, name-and-form; by means of name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases; by means of the six sense bases as condition, contact; by means of contact as condition, feeling; by means of feeling as condition, craving; by means of craving as condition, clinging; by means of clinging as condition, existence; by means of existence as condition, birth; by means of birth as condition, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come to be. Such is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.”
At Sāvatthī.

“Bhikkhus, if there were no gratification in the earth element, beings would not be enamored with the earth element. But because there is gratification in the earth element, beings are enamored with it.”
“Bhikkhus, if there were no danger in the earth element, beings would not experience revulsion toward the earth element.
But because there is danger in the earth element, beings experience revulsion toward the earth element.
Bhikkhus, if there were no escape from the earth element, beings would not escape from the earth element.”
But because, monks, there is an escape from the earth element, therefore beings escape from the earth element.
If, monks, there were no gratification in the water element ... [and so on] ...
if, monks, there were no gratification in the fire element ... [and so on] ...
If, monks, there were no gratification in the air element, beings would not become infatuated with the air element.
But because there is gratification in the air element, monks, beings become infatuated with the air element.
If, monks, there were no danger in the air element, beings would not become disenchanted with the air element.
But because, monks, there is a danger in the air element, beings become disenchanted with the air element.
If, monks, there were no escape from the air element, beings would not escape from the air element.
But because, monks, there is an escape from the air element, beings escape from the air element.

“Bhikkhus, as long as these beings have not directly known, as they really are, the gratification as gratification, the danger as danger, and the escape as escape regarding these four elements, so long, bhikkhus,
have these beings not been released from this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, from this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans.”
They dwelt having emerged, detached, and utterly freed from them with a mind for which the boundaries of perception had vanished.

But when, monks, beings directly knew these four elements as they really are— in their gratification as gratification, in their danger as danger, and in the escape from them as escape— then, monks, those beings...
“Having emerged from the world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, from this generation with its recluses and brahmins,
its devas and humans, they dwell with minds that are detached, disjoined, and completely liberated, having transcended the realm of Māra. This is the fourth.

Saṁyutta Nikāya 14.34 (SN 14.34, PTS SN ii 173) 4. Catutthavagga Ekantadukkhasutta (The Discourse on Being Exclusively Suffering) “Bhikkhus, form is exclusively suffering; feeling is exclusively suffering; perception is exclusively suffering; volitional formations are exclusively suffering; consciousness is exclusively suffering. Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the instructed noble disciple experiences revulsion towards form, revulsion towards feeling, revulsion towards perception, revulsion towards volitional formations, and revulsion towards consciousness. Experiencing revulsion, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, [his mind] is liberated. When it is liberated, there comes the knowledge: ‘It is liberated. He understands: ‘Destroyed is birth, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.’”
At Sāvatthī.
"Bhikkhus, if this earth element were exclusively painful—overcome by pain, beset by pain, and not relieved of pain—beings would not become attached to the earth element.
But because, bhikkhus, the earth element is pleasant, overcome by pleasure, beset by pleasure, and not relieved of pain, therefore beings become attached to the earth element."
If, monks, this water element here ...
if, monks, this fire element here ...
if, monks, this air element here were exclusively suffering, beset by suffering, overwhelmed by suffering, and not touched by pleasure, beings would not be enamored of the air element.
But because, monks, the air element is pleasant, accompanied by pleasure, permeated by pleasure, and not permeated by pain, therefore beings are infatuated with the air element.
If, monks, this earth element were exclusively pleasant, accompanied by pleasure, permeated by pleasure, and not permeated by pain, beings would not become disenchanted with the earth element.
But because, monks, the earth element is suffering, beset by suffering, overwhelmed by suffering, and not overwhelmed by pleasure, therefore beings grow weary of the earth element.
And if this water element, monks...
[and] if this fire element, monks... [is likewise so].
“Bhikkhus, if this air element were exclusively pleasant, associated with pleasure, steeped in pleasure, and not steeped in pain, beings would not experience revulsion toward the air element.
But because, bhikkhus, the air element is painful, associated with pain, steeped in pain, and not steeped in pleasure, therefore beings experience revulsion toward the air element.
The fifth.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 14.35 (SN 14.35, PTS SN ii 174) 4. Catutthavagga Abhinandasutta “Bhikkhus, when one delights in form, welcomes it, and remains attached to it, one is bound by that delight. When one delights in feeling, welcomes it, and remains attached to it, one is bound by that delight. When one delights in perception, welcomes it, and remains attached to it, one is bound by that delight. When one delights in volitional formations, welcomes them, and remains attached to them, one is bound by that delight. When one delights in consciousness, welcomes it, and remains attached to it, one is bound by that delight. “Bhikkhus, when one does not delight in form, does not welcome it, and does not remain attached to it, one is liberated from that delight. When one does not delight in feeling, does not welcome it, and does not remain attached to it, one is liberated from that delight. When one does not delight in perception, does not welcome it, and does not remain attached to it, one is liberated from that delight. When one does not delight in volitional formations, does not welcome them, and does not remain attached to them, one is liberated from that delight. When one does not delight in consciousness, does not welcome it, and does not remain attached to it, one is liberated from that delight.”
At Sāvatthī. “Monks, whoever delights in the earth element, he delights in suffering.
Whoever delights in suffering, I say that he is not liberated from suffering.”
Whoever delights in the water element … whoever delights in the fire element … whoever delights in the air element, that person delights in suffering.
"Whoever delights in suffering, I say, is not liberated from suffering.
But whoever, monks, does not delight in the earth element, he does not delight in suffering.
Whoever does not delight in suffering, I say, is liberated from suffering."
Whoever does not delight in the water element …pe… whoever does not delight in the fire element … whoever does not delight in the air element, he does not delight in suffering.
“He who does not delight in suffering, him I call one who is fully liberated from suffering. Thus it was said.
The sixth.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 14.36. (SN 14.36, PTS SN ii 175)
4. The Fourth Chapter:
The Discourse on Arising.
At Sāvatthī, he was staying there.

“Bhikkhus, whatever is the arising, the persistence, the production, and the manifestation of the earth element— that is the arising of suffering, the persistence of diseases, and the manifestation of aging and death.
Whatever is [the arising, the persistence, the production, and the manifestation] of the water element … of the fire element …”

Whatever is the arising, the persistence, the production, and the manifestation of the air element—that is the arising of suffering, the persistence of diseases, and the manifestation of aging and death.
But whatever, monks, is the cessation, the subsiding, and the passing away of the earth element—that is the cessation of suffering, the subsiding of diseases, and the passing away of aging and death.
Whatever [is the cessation] of the water element... [and so on].

Whatever is the cessation, the subsiding, and the passing away of the fire element … or of the air element, that is the cessation of suffering, the subsiding of diseases, and the passing away of aging and death.
The seventh.

Saṁyutta Nikāya 14.37 (SN 14.37, PTS SN ii 175) 4. Catutthavagga Samaṇabrāhmaṇasutta “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of ascetics and brahmins to be found existing in the world. What four? The one who is immersed in the mud and wallows in the mud; the one who has emerged from the mud but is still smeared with it; the one who has emerged from the mud and is no longer smeared with it, and stands with his feet on solid ground; and the one who, having crossed over and gone beyond, stands on firm ground, a brahmin who has reached the further shore, a conqueror, a noble one, a tamed one, one who has laid down the burden, one who has accomplished his task, one whose fetters are destroyed, one who has attained perfect knowledge, one freed through final knowledge. And how, bhikkhus, is one an ascetic and brahmin who is immersed in the mud and wallows in the mud? Here, someone is reborn in hell, in the animal realm, or in the sphere of afflicted spirits. This is called an ascetic and brahmin who is immersed in the mud and wallows in the mud. And how is one an ascetic and brahmin who has emerged from the mud but is still smeared with it? Here, someone is reborn among human beings or in the deva worlds. This is called an ascetic and brahmin who has emerged from the mud but is still smeared with it. And how is one an ascetic and brahmin who has emerged from the mud and is no longer smeared with it, and stands with his feet on solid ground?

Here, someone is a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination. This is called an ascetic and brahmin who has emerged from the mud and is no longer smeared with it, and stands with his feet on solid ground. And how is one an ascetic and brahmin who, having crossed over and gone beyond, stands on firm ground, a brahmin who has reached the further shore, a conqueror, a noble one, a tamed one, one who has laid down the burden, one who has accomplished his task, one whose fetters are destroyed, one who has attained perfect knowledge, one freed through final knowledge? Here, someone is an arahant, one whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained the true goal, destroyed the fetters of existence, and is liberated through final knowledge. This is called an ascetic and brahmin who, having crossed over and gone beyond, stands on firm ground, a brahmin who has reached the further shore, a conqueror, a noble one, a tamed one, one who has laid down the burden, one who has accomplished his task, one whose fetters are destroyed, one who has attained perfect knowledge, one freed through final knowledge.”
At Sāvatthī, the Blessed One was staying.
“Monks, there are these four elements. Which four?
The earth element, the water element, the fire element,
and the air element. For whatever ascetics or brahmins, monks, do not understand as they really are the gratification, the danger, and the escape in regard to these four elements,
those ascetics or brahmins, monks, are not considered ascetics among ascetics, nor brahmins among brahmins.
They are esteemed as brahmins, yet those venerable ones do not,
by realizing it for themselves with direct knowledge,

enter and dwell in the goal of the ascetic life or the goal of the brahmin life in this very world. But whoever, monks, among these ascetics or brahmins, understands as they really are the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding these four elements—
"And those recluses or brahmins, monks, are indeed reckoned as recluses among recluses and as brahmins among brahmins;
moreover, those venerable ones dwell having themselves realized, through direct higher knowledge, and having attained, the goal of the recluse and the goal of the brahmin in this very life."
The Eighth.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 14.38 (SN 14.38, PTS SN ii 176) 4.
The Fourth Chapter
The Second Discourse on Ascetics and Brahmins.
At Sāvatthī, the Blessed One was staying.
“Bhikkhus, there are these four elements.”

Which four? The earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element. For whatever ascetics or brahmins, monks, do not understand as they really are the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding these four elements... [as before] ...they are not arahants, they are not one who has reached the final goal in this very life. But those ascetics or brahmins who understand as they really are the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding these four elements... they are arahants, they are ones who have reached the final goal in this very life. This is the fourth case. These, monks, are the four cases. What four? There are ascetics and brahmins who do not understand as they really are the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding this body with its consciousness and all external phenomena; yet they claim: "We shall make known the unmade, the unarisen, the unborn, the unproduced, the unconditioned. This is the first case. There are ascetics and brahmins who understand as they really are the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding this body with its consciousness and all external phenomena; yet they claim: "We shall make known the unmade, the unarisen, the unborn, the unproduced, the unconditioned. This is the second case. There are ascetics and brahmins who do not understand as they really are the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding this body with its consciousness and all external phenomena; yet they do not claim: "We shall make known the unmade, the unarisen, the unborn, the unproduced, the unconditioned. This is the third case. There are ascetics and brahmins who understand as they really are the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding this body with its consciousness and all external phenomena; and they claim: "We shall make known the unmade, the unarisen, the unborn, the unproduced, the unconditioned. This is the fourth case. These, monks, are the four cases. What four? There are ascetics and brahmins who do not understand as they really are the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding this body with its consciousness and all external phenomena; yet they claim: "The Tathāgata exists after death. This is the first case. There are ascetics and brahmins who understand as they really are the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding this body with its consciousness and all external phenomena; yet they claim: "The Tathāgata does not exist after death. This is the second case. There are ascetics and brahmins who do not understand as they really are the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding this body with its consciousness and all external phenomena; yet they do not claim: "The Tathāgata exists after death. This is the third case. There are ascetics and brahmins who understand as they really are the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding this body with its consciousness and all external phenomena; and they claim: "The Tathāgata exists after death. This is the fourth case. These, monks, are the four cases. What four? There are ascetics and brahmins who do not understand as they really are the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding this body with its consciousness and all external phenomena; yet they claim: "The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death. This is the first case. There are ascetics and brahmins who understand as they really are the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding this body with its consciousness and all external phenomena; yet they claim: "The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death. This is the second case. There are ascetics and brahmins who do not understand as they really are the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding this body with its consciousness and all external phenomena; yet they do not claim: "The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death. This is the third case. There are ascetics and brahmins who understand as they really are the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding this body with its consciousness and all external phenomena; and they claim: "The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death. This is the fourth case. These, monks, are the four cases. What four? There are ascetics and brahmins who do not understand as they really are the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding this body with its consciousness and all external phenomena; yet they claim: "The self and the world are eternal. This is the first case. There are ascetics and brahmins who understand as they really are the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding this body with its consciousness and all external phenomena; yet they claim: "The self and the world are non-eternal. This is the second case. There are ascetics and brahmins who do not understand as they really are the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding this body with its consciousness and all external phenomena; yet they do not claim: "The self and the world are eternal. This is the third case. There are ascetics and brahmins who understand as they really are the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding this body with its consciousness and all external phenomena; and they claim: "The self and the world are eternal. This is the fourth case. These, monks, are the four cases. What four? There are ascetics and brahmins who do not understand as they really are the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding this body with its consciousness and all external phenomena; yet they claim: "The self and the world are finite. This is the first case. There are ascetics and brahmins who understand as they really are the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding this body with its consciousness and all external phenomena; yet they claim: "The self and the world are infinite. This is the second case. There are ascetics and brahmins who do not understand as they really are the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding this body with its consciousness and all external phenomena; yet they do not claim: "The self and the world are finite. This is the third case. There are ascetics and brahmins who understand as they really are the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding this body with its consciousness and all external phenomena; and they claim: "The self and the world are finite. This is the fourth case. These, monks, are the four cases. What four? There are ascetics and brahmins who do not understand as they really are the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding this body with its consciousness and all external phenomena; yet they claim: "The self and the world are both finite and infinite. This is the first case. There are ascetics and brahmins who understand as they really are the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding this body with its consciousness and all external phenomena; yet they claim: "The self and the world are neither finite nor infinite. This is the second case. There are ascetics and brahmins who do not understand as they really are the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding this body with its consciousness and all external phenomena; yet they do not claim: "The self and the world are both finite and infinite. This is the third case. There are ascetics and brahmins who understand as they really are the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding this body with its consciousness and all external phenomena; and they claim: "The self and the world are both finite and infinite. This is the fourth case. These, monks, are the four cases. What four? There are ascetics and brahmins who do not understand as they really are the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding this body with its consciousness and all external phenomena; yet they claim: "The soul is the same as the body. This is the first case. Saṁyutta Nikāya 14.39 (SN 14.39, PTS SN ii 176) 4. Catutthavagga Tatiyasamaṇabrāhmaṇasutta The Third Discourse on Ascetics and Brahmins “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of ascetics and brahmins to be found existing in the world. What four? “The one who is intent on the present life, not intent on the future life; the one who is intent on the future life, not intent on the present life; the one who is intent neither on the present life nor on the future life; and the one who is intent both on the present life and on the future life. “And how, bhikkhus, is an ascetic or brahmin intent on the present life, not intent on the future life? Here, someone maintains this view: ‘There is nothing given, nothing offered, nothing sacrificed; there is no fruit or result of good and bad actions; there is no this world, no other world; there is no mother, no father; there are no beings spontaneously born; there are in the world no ascetics and brahmins of right conduct and right practice who, having realized this world and the other world for themselves by direct knowledge, make them known to others. “This, bhikkhus, is called an ascetic or brahmin intent on the present life, not intent on the future life. “And how, bhikkhus, is an ascetic or brahmin intent on the future life, not intent on the present life? Here, someone maintains this view:

‘When one acts or makes others act, when one mutilates or makes others mutilate, when one tortures or makes others inflict torture, when one inflicts sorrow or makes others inflict sorrow, when one oppresses or makes others inflict oppression, when one intimidates or makes others inflict intimidation, when one destroys life, takes what is not given, breaks into houses, plunders wealth, commits burglary, ambushes highways, seduces another’s wife, utters falsehood—when one engages in such kamma, after death, with the breakup of the body, one becomes a deva. “This, bhikkhus, is called an ascetic or brahmin intent on the future life, not intent on the present life. “And how, bhikkhus, is an ascetic or brahmin intent neither on the present life nor on the future life? Here, someone maintains this view: ‘When one acts or makes others act... [as above] ...utters falsehood—when one engages in such kamma, one experiences the result here and now, or one experiences it after death, or one experiences it at some time. “This, bhikkhus, is called an ascetic or brahmin intent neither on the present life nor on the future life. “And how, bhikkhus, is an ascetic or brahmin intent both on the present life and on the future life? Here, someone maintains this view: ‘When one acts or makes others act... [as above] ...utters falsehood—when one engages in such kamma, one experiences the result here and now, or one experiences it after death, or one experiences it at some time. “This, bhikkhus, is called an ascetic or brahmin intent both on the present life and on the future life. “These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of ascetics and brahmins to be found existing in the world.”
[The Blessed One] was dwelling at Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, whatever recluses or brahmins do not understand the earth element, do not understand the origin of the earth element,
do not understand the cessation of the earth element, and do not understand the practice leading to the cessation of the earth element … [as before] …”
They do not understand the water element;
they do not understand the fire element;
they do not understand the air element; they do not understand the origin of the air element; they do not understand the cessation of the air element.
Those who do not understand the practice leading to the cessation of the air element, monks,
are neither ascetics among ascetics nor brahmins among brahmins.
Furthermore, those venerable ones do not, by realizing it for themselves with direct knowledge, enter and dwell in the goal of the ascetic life or the goal of the brahmin life in this very life.

"Monks, whatever ascetics or brahmins understand the earth element, understand the origin of the earth element, understand the cessation of the earth element, and understand the practice leading to the cessation of the earth element...
and whatever ascetics or brahmins, monks... understand the water element..."
They understand the fire element;
they understand the air element; they understand the origin of the air element; they understand the cessation of the air element;
and they understand the way leading to the cessation of the air element—those, monks, are indeed the ascetics or brahmins [who truly are such].
Or those who are truly ascetics among ascetics and truly brahmins among brahmins;
and these venerable ones, having realized for themselves through direct knowledge in this very life the goal of asceticism and the goal of brahminhood, dwell having attained them.

and delighting in arising—
